name: Miswak / chew stick
lead: Miswak is a traditional tooth-cleaning stick made from the twigs, stems or roots of the Salvadora persica tree, also called the arak or peelu tree. One end is chewed or peeled to expose fibres that act as bristles. Neem twigs (Azadirachta indica) serve a similar purpose in parts of South Asia, where they are known as datun. [1][2][3]

The stick has been used for centuries across the Middle East, Africa and South Asia, and it holds religious significance in Islamic tradition. [3][4] People use it for oral hygiene, fresher breath and, in some accounts, a whiter and polished look to the teeth. [1][5]

Reviews of the clinical literature report that miswak use, alone or beside a toothbrush, is associated with reductions in plaque and gingival inflammation, though the trials are small and varied in design. Evidence that it whitens teeth is thinner and comes largely from descriptive accounts. [6][7][8]

Sold as a traditional hygiene product; also an ingredient in some toothpastes and mouthwashes [3]

paras: A miswak is a small twig or root segment whose outer bark is peeled from one end to expose natural fibres. It is moved over the teeth and gums, and the used end can be trimmed to make a fresh brushing surface. [3][1] Extracts of Salvadora persica are also used in mouthwash, toothpaste, varnish and chewing gum formulations. [8][3]

Chew sticks are among the oldest known oral hygiene tools. Reviews describe the practice as ancient and long established in many regions. [1][4] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, dates chew sticks to Babylonian and Egyptian contexts thousands of years ago, though such dating claims vary by source. [22]

In Islamic tradition, hadith attributed to the Prophet Muhammad recommend the miswak at times such as before prayer or ablution, on waking and when travelling, and it is regarded as a practice of ritual cleanliness. [3] The World Health Organization recommended chewing sticks in 1986, and a 2000 international consensus report concluded further research was needed. [3]

The stick acts mechanically, with its fibres removing plaque and debris, and may act chemically through plant compounds. Salvadora persica contains benzyl isothiocyanate, which has shown strong activity against Gram-negative bacteria in laboratory tests. [9] Reviews list reported antibacterial, anticariogenic and antiplaque properties, along with minerals and antioxidants. [4][10][11] A randomised study reported that rinsing with miswak extract kept plaque pH elevated for longer than water after an acid challenge. [12]

An evidence-based review covering studies from 2010 to 2020 reported that all included studies found a positive effect of miswak, across forms including chewing sticks, mouthwash, toothpaste, essential oil and varnish. [6] A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials assessed miswak and neem sticks used with a toothbrush for plaque and gingivitis in adults. [7]

A 2019 meta-analysis compared Salvadora persica mouthrinse with chlorhexidine and placebo for plaque and cariogenic bacteria. [13] Randomised trials have tested a miswak-extract toothpaste for gingival inflammation, a 40 percent miswak mouthwash versus 0.12 percent chlorhexidine for gingivitis, and fluoridated miswak against toothbrushing with fluoridated toothpaste for plaque removal. [14][15][16] A clinical trial examined chemical effects of the sticks on plaque, gingival microbiota and gingival inflammation. [17] Wikipedia notes that miswak extract showed lower antibacterial activity than chlorhexidine and some disinfectants in comparisons it cites. [3]

Other work includes survey studies of oral hygiene practices in Saudi Arabia and halitosis in Kuwait, and laboratory studies of antibacterial activity against oral bacteria. [18][19][20] These studies concern oral health outcomes. No controlled trial was found that measured tooth whitening or appearance ratings after miswak use.

The reviews generally describe miswak as safe and inexpensive. [2][4] A letter in the British Dental Journal addresses misuse of miswak. [21] Some reviews note that study quality varies and that more rigorous trials are needed. [6][7] Wikipedia's account of the practice notes that several traditional benefit claims, such as strengthening gums and easing toothache, lack citations. [3]

Grokipedia and review articles describe traditional use to whiten and polish teeth and to freshen breath, and one review says ancient Arabs used it to whiten and polish the teeth. [22][5] Grokipedia states that studies support mild whitening through surface stain removal, but that statement was not traced to a controlled whitening trial. [22]

card.summary: A traditional twig toothbrush from the arak tree; small trials link it to less plaque, but whitening claims are untested.
card.note: Trials measure plaque and gum health, not tooth colour; study quality is mixed.

quick.overview:
Miswak is a chewing stick cut from the Salvadora persica tree, used for centuries in the Middle East, Africa and South Asia and valued in Islamic tradition. The frayed end works as a natural brush.

Reviews report reductions in plaque and gum inflammation in small trials, and it is also used for fresher breath and in traditional accounts for whiter teeth. No controlled trial of whitening was found.
quick.mechanism: The fibres scrub plaque from the teeth, and plant compounds such as benzyl isothiocyanate have shown antibacterial activity in laboratory tests. A trial also reported higher plaque pH after rinsing with the extract.
quick.risks: Reviews describe it as low-risk and cheap, but they also note variable study quality and the need for larger trials. Comparisons cited on Wikipedia show lower antibacterial activity than chlorhexidine. A dental-journal letter discusses misuse of the stick.
